input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-452: Systems Programming. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Application of operating system concepts to the design of hardware interfaces for a multiprogramming environment. Laboratory work includes the development of a multiprogramming (optionally, multiprocessing) kernel with system call and interrupt handling facilities, and the building of device drivers for a variety of peripheral devices. This course provides extensive experience with those aspects of systems programming that deal directly with the hardware interface. A significant team programming project is a major component of this course. Prerequisites: CSCI-352 or (4003-334 and 4003-345) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-xv6-book]
The xv6 book explains processes, system calls, traps, page tables, scheduling, locking, file systems, devices, concurrency, and isolation in a small Unix-like kernel. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits. The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context. Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state. The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates. Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.

[riscv-unprivileged]
The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while the remaining integer registers hold software-visible values. Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers. Store instructions transfer register data to memory. Branch and jump instructions change control flow. Exceptions report conditions that require a defined transfer of control. Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed. Architecture analysis preserves data dependencies, control dependencies, and architectural state.

[rit-csci-452]
Application of operating system concepts to the design of hardware interfaces for a multiprogramming environment. Laboratory work includes the development of a multiprogramming (optionally, multiprocessing) kernel with system call and interrupt handling facilities, and the building of device drivers for a variety of peripheral devices. This course provides extensive experience with those aspects of systems programming that deal directly with the hardware interface. A significant team programming project is a major component of this course. Prerequisites: CSCI-352 or (4003-334 and 4003-345) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

beats.claim: A multiprogramming environment allows multiple processes to execute concurrently by sharing system resources while maintaining isolation.
beats.example: A server running multiple web requests simultaneously uses separate address spaces for each process to prevent memory corruption.
beats.title: 1. Multiprogramming Environment Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram showing three isolated process bubbles sharing a central CPU and memory bus, with arrows indicating context switches.

beats.claim: A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources to function as an independent unit of scheduling.
beats.example: Each running application maintains its own stack, heap, and open file descriptors, preventing data leakage between applications.
beats.title: 2. Process Definition and State
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen comparison of a process structure containing an address space block, execution state register, and resource list.

beats.claim: The operating system enforces a strict boundary between user mode and privileged kernel code to protect system integrity.
beats.example: A user program cannot directly modify the page table or interrupt controller registers without triggering a protection fault.
beats.title: 3. User Mode vs. Privileged Kernel Mode
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a two-tiered architecture diagram with a 'User Mode' zone and a 'Kernel Mode' zone separated by a security boundary line.

beats.claim: A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service to perform privileged operations safely.
beats.example: Calling read() from a user program triggers a trap that switches execution to the kernel's file system driver.
beats.title: 4. System Call Mechanism
beats.visualDirection: Draw a flowchart showing user code invoking a system call, transitioning to kernel code, and returning control with results.

beats.claim: A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt without losing execution context.
beats.example: When an interrupt occurs, the CPU automatically saves the instruction pointer, registers, and flags to a stack frame for later restoration.
beats.title: 5. Trap Handling and Processor State
beats.visualDirection: Display a stack diagram showing saved registers and the instruction pointer pushed onto the kernel stack during a trap.

beats.claim: Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits to enable safe memory management.
beats.example: A virtual address is decomposed into a page number and offset, then translated by the MMU using the page table to locate the actual physical frame.
beats.title: 6. Virtual to Physical Memory Mapping
beats.visualDirection: Show a two-column table mapping virtual page numbers to physical page numbers, with checkmarks indicating read/write/execute permissions.

beats.claim: The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior.
beats.example: Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers, while store instructions transfer register data to memory according to defined rules.
beats.title: 7. RISC-V ISA and Memory Operations
beats.visualDirection: Present a side-by-side comparison of a load instruction and a store instruction with register and memory operand labels.

beats.claim: Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed, preserving data dependencies and architectural state.
beats.example: A compiler or CPU may reorder independent memory accesses for performance, but must maintain the relative order of dependent operations.
beats.title: 8. Memory Ordering and Dependencies
beats.visualDirection: Show a sequence of memory operations with arrows indicating dependency chains and ordering constraints between them.

beats.claim: Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state, preventing race conditions in kernel services.
beats.example: A mutex lock ensures that only one process can modify the process control block at a time during context switching.
beats.title: 9. Locks and Concurrency Invariants
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a lock acquisition and release cycle with two concurrent threads waiting for and releasing a shared resource.

beats.claim: Systems programming requires verifying that hardware interfaces correctly handle interrupts, manage memory mappings, and enforce isolation in a multiprogramming environment.
beats.example: A driver must validate interrupt flags, update page table entries, and acquire locks before modifying shared device registers.
beats.title: 10. Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a checklist with checkboxes for: interrupt handling, page table validation, lock acquisition, and isolation verification.

learningObjectives: Define the operational boundaries between user mode and privileged kernel mode in a multiprogramming environment.
Explain how system calls and traps transfer control from user code to kernel services while preserving processor state.
Apply hardware interface design principles by mapping virtual addresses to physical memory using page tables and managing concurrent access with locks

The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Consider this worked case: Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers, while store instructions transfer register data to memory according to defined rules. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Consider this worked case: When an interrupt occurs, the CPU automatically saves the instruction pointer, registers, and flags to a stack frame for later restoration. Begin by framing 1. Multiprogramming Environment Overview as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. With the foundation in place, examine how 3. User Mode vs. Privileged Kernel Mode operates in a concrete sequence.
